title: El efecto de los inicializadores: una auditoría de grafos en cinco repositorios de IA
summary:
El efecto de los inicializadores: una auditoría de grafos en cinco repositorios de IA

Fecha de publicación del análisis: 28 de octubre de 2026. Esta es una medición descriptiva de cinco paquetes Python seleccionados intencionalmente. No es un ranking de las cinco startups más grandes ni una muestra estadísticamente representativa.

Introducción

Platino Labs publicó un análisis reproducible de grafos de imports para cinco proyectos del ecosistema de IA. El Data Room v2 contiene el calculador, las cinco proyecciones públicas graph-input/1 y los resultados de sensibilidad. El Release v1 conserva la metodología y los resultados base, incluidos los commits evaluados.

La pregunta es acotada: ¿cuánto cambia el grafo estático de imports cuando se omite únicamente la expansión hacia archivos __init__.py ancestrales? No medimos vulnerabilidades, calidad general, riesgo empresarial ni comportamiento de ejecución.

Hallazgo principal: LangChain cambia bajo la ablación

En el snapshot de langchain, el grafo base contiene 2 componentes fuertemente conexas (SCC) cíclicas; la mayor contiene 19 módulos. Al conservar los destinos directos resueltos y omitir solo la expansión ancestral de __init__.py, el grafo proyectado contiene 0 SCC cíclicas.

Esto demuestra que el resultado del grafo estático es sensible a esa regla de construcción de aristas. No demuestra que los ciclos desaparezcan en ejecución, que el empaquetado sea la causa raíz ni que exista un defecto de rendimiento. La ablación identifica una pregunta para una auditoría dinámica posterior; no la responde.

LlamaIndex muestra otra forma: se mantienen 4 SCC cíclicas en ambos grafos, aunque la mayor pasa de 334 a 239 módulos dentro de un universo de 480 módulos. El ciclo mayor se reduce, pero no desaparece. Tampoco es, por sí solo, una medida de riesgo o deuda técnica.

Resultados por snapshot

Repositorio / paquete Commit medido SCC base LOC SCC / 10.000 LOC SCC sin expansión de inicializadores Tamaño de la SCC mayor: base → ablación
vLLM · vllm 7e3e3f6ab652550fdefecd8e9823394fd8e51950 23 959.216 0,240 8 1.648 → 1.394
LangChain · langchain facf2788ae1f60c62f2397d15698237c405a5f05 2 13.352 1,498 0 19 → 0
Transformers · transformers 95bafdcccfffe17ec383999fc39273867b11385e 8 996.643 0,080 6 176 → 169
BentoML · bentoml 0aa1aea52b63b82100ff93675eff25f6428fb841 5 38.508 1,298 4 78 → 42
LlamaIndex · llama_index 619d74664e8404612038bc15a1a40c686037277c 4 61.322 0,652 4 334 → 239

LOC cuenta líneas físicas con tokens Python y excluye comentarios y líneas vacías. La densidad es SCC cíclicas / LOC × 10.000; sirve para describir estos snapshots, no como puntuación de calidad ni como probabilidad de fallo. La muestra fue seleccionada intencionalmente y no permite inferir prevalencia en toda la industria.

Metodología reproducible

El calculador forma un grafo dirigido de módulos Python y obtiene sus SCC con el algoritmo de Tarjan. Una SCC se cuenta como cíclica si contiene más de un módulo o un auto-bucle. Se excluyen imports type_checking; se conservan los demás tipos incluidos en la proyección.

Para reproducir la ablación, descarga los activos del Release v2 y ejecuta, con Python 3.10 o posterior:

python3 calculate_arch_index.py public_graph_bentoml_0aa1aea5.json --graph-sensitivity > graph_sensitivity_bentoml.json
python3 calculate_arch_index.py public_graph_langchain_facf2788.json --graph-sensitivity > graph_sensitivity_langchain.json
python3 calculate_arch_index.py public_graph_llamaindex_619d7466.json --graph-sensitivity > graph_sensitivity_llama_index.json
python3 calculate_arch_index.py public_graph_transformers_95bafdcc.json --graph-sensitivity > graph_sensitivity_transformers.json
python3 calculate_arch_index.py public_graph_vllm_7e3e3f6a.json --graph-sensitivity > graph_sensitivity_vllm.json

Cada resultado incluye el SHA-256 de los bytes de su proyección de entrada. Las proyecciones omiten snippets de código y raíces locales; el modo --graph-sensitivity no vuelve a hashear los archivos fuente y declara source_bytes_verified: false. Para reproducir los resultados base con verificación contra los fuentes, sigue las instrucciones y los commits completos del Release v1.

Por qué importa — y qué no afirma

Los ciclos y el tamaño de sus componentes describen una propiedad topológica del grafo estático calculado. Pueden orientar una revisión de límites entre módulos y pruebas posteriores, pero estos datos no miden tiempos de carga, fallos de importación, complejidad de testing, vulnerabilidades ni deuda técnica. Para afirmar cualquiera de esas cosas hacen falta instrumentos, ventanas y controles específicos.

title: LoRA on a 16 GB card: what fits and what does not
summary:
A 7B model is the honest ceiling for LoRA fine-tuning on a 16 GB consumer card, not because anything bigger throws an error, but because a 14B model silently spills into system memory and runs 50 times slower without ever reporting a failure.

Key takeaways

  • 7B is the real ceiling on an RTX 5070 Ti at LoRA rank 16, sequence length 512, batch size 1: 11,897.9 MiB peak, well inside the card's 16,303 MiB.
  • 14B completed without a raised exception in both tested conditions, but peak VRAM read 22,189.8 MiB (136% of the card) and 17,470.9 MiB (107%) - both over the physical limit, through Windows' silent system-memory fallback.
  • The cost of that fallback is severe: 21.7 seconds per training step at 14B against 0.4 seconds at 7B, roughly 51 times slower, with no error message anywhere.
  • Gradient checkpointing is close to free at 7B and below - same or less time, meaningfully less memory - but does not rescue 14B: it leaves the model still over the limit and makes the step 59% slower, not faster.
  • The registered hypothesis that checkpointing moves the ceiling up a tier is rejected; the wording of the first kill-gate also needed correcting, because "did not throw an out-of-memory error" turned out to be the wrong proxy for "fits".

Why doesn't "no error" mean "it fits"?

I pre-registered two kill-gates on an RTX 5070 Ti, 16,303 MiB of physical VRAM: whether a 14B Qwen2.5-Instruct model, loaded in 4-bit with a LoRA adapter, completes one real training step without a raised CUDA out-of-memory exception, and whether gradient checkpointing moves that ceiling up by at least one tested size, following the same discipline described in why I pre-register a kill-gate for every experiment. Neither 14B run threw an exception. By the literal wording of the first gate, it fired - 14B "fits". But torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() reported 22,189.8 MiB without checkpointing, 5,887 MiB above the card's physical limit, and the step took 21.7 seconds instead of the sub-second range every smaller model showed. Windows ships a driver-level system-memory fallback policy that lets CUDA allocations succeed past a card's physical limit by quietly paging into ordinary RAM instead of raising an error, and nothing in the console said so. The gate measured the wrong thing: "did not throw an exception" is not the same claim as "fits in 16 GB", and only comparing the allocator figure against the card's actual VRAM, plus noticing the 50x time cliff, exposed the gap.

What did the clean numbers actually look like?

Three of the four sizes behaved exactly as expected. Without checkpointing, 1.5B peaked at 4,000.7 MiB, 3B at 6,749.0 MiB, 7B at 11,897.9 MiB - all comfortably under 16,303 MiB, all completing a forward-backward-optimizer step in under half a second. 7B used 73% of the card's VRAM at rank 16, sequence length 512, batch size 1, with real room to spare. Full numbers for all eight configurations sit in the frozen plan and results in the public experiment repository. Enabling gradient checkpointing lowered every one of those three figures - 2,855.5 MiB, 4,490.8 MiB and 9,709.9 MiB respectively - at essentially no time cost: 7B ran in the same 0.425 seconds either way, 3B cost 25% more time for a third less memory. The 1.5B timing is excluded from this comparison because it ran first in the script and likely carries a one-time CUDA initialisation cost. The honest ceiling for this exact setup, Qwen2.5-Instruct, 4-bit base, LoRA rank 16, one sequence of 512 tokens, batch size 1, is 7B. Push any of those variables up and the real number moves down, not up.

Does gradient checkpointing rescue the 14B case?

No. With checkpointing enabled, 14B still reported 17,470.9 MiB, 1,168 MiB over the card's physical limit - smaller than the 5,887 MiB overflow without checkpointing, but still spilling into system memory, not fitting inside it. The step time went the wrong direction: 34.5 seconds, 59% slower than the 21.7 seconds without checkpointing. Checkpointing buys memory by deleting intermediate activations during the forward pass and recomputing them during backward, and that recompute cost is normally hidden by the time saved from avoiding memory pressure, which is exactly why it helped 7B and below for free. Once the card is already paging to system RAM, the saved memory only shrinks an already-severe penalty instead of removing it, and the extra computation adds straight on top. The registered hypothesis, that checkpointing moves the ceiling up by at least one tested tier, is rejected. On this card, for this model family, checkpointing is a real, close-to-free lever below the ceiling, not a way past it.

FAQ

Does this mean a 16 GB card can never run a 14B model?

Not for training, no, not with this exact setup. A smaller rank, a shorter sequence, a smaller LoRA target set, or a more aggressive quantisation scheme could plausibly bring a 14B model under the limit; none of those were tested here. For inference rather than training, the memory math is different again and was not measured in this experiment.

Why trust torch's reported VRAM figure at all, if it can be wrong?

It is not wrong about what it allocates - torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() reports real tensor memory the CUDA allocator granted, honestly. What it does not tell you is whether that memory was physically on the card or transparently paged to system RAM by the driver. Comparing the figure against the card's known physical limit, rather than trusting the absence of an exception, is what catches the difference.

Why only test rank 16 and batch size 1?

Those are close to the smallest realistic defaults most people reach for first. Testing a single point cleanly, rather than sweeping many configurations in one pass, keeps the registered claim specific and checkable. A larger rank or batch size sweep is a legitimate follow-up, not something this experiment's kill-gates covered.

Where do the numbers come from?

Every figure in this piece is read directly from results.json in the registered experiment, not estimated or rounded from memory. The frozen plan, the full experiment code, and the raw per-run output all sit in the public repository linked above, so the eight numbers in the table can be checked against the source instead of taken on trust.

References

  • Edward J. Hu, Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis, Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li, Shean Wang, Lu Wang, Weizhu Chen. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models, 2021. arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685

title: Late Edition: Giving OCR Text a Second Look 📰
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

Late Edition: Giving OCR Text a Second Look 📰

What I Built

Newspaper scans can hold valuable information, but getting that information into usable text isn't always straightforward. OCR can misread characters, distort words, and turn a perfectly readable page into a messy block of text.

For Week 4, I built Late Edition, a Python prototype that explores how language models can help correct OCR text while keeping potentially risky changes in check.

The idea was to let a model suggest repairs without automatically trusting everything it produces.

Late Edition takes OCR text, splits it into chunks, and sends those chunks to a selected Gemma model. Before accepting a proposed correction, it runs a set of deterministic checks to decide whether the change is safe enough to keep.

It can also generate an HTML report showing the original text, accepted edits, and rejected suggestions.

The goal isn't to produce a verified historical transcription. It's to explore a more cautious way of using AI for text correction.

Demo

HTML report: [Add a sample report link or screenshot]

The report is designed to make the correction process easier to inspect, including changes the system chose not to accept.

Code

GitHub repository: https://github.com/ali-scribe/late-edition

The main implementation is organized around the correction checks in guard.py and the report generation in report.py.

How I Built It

Late Edition is built with Python and uses a selected Gemma model through Google's hosted Gemini API.

The workflow has three main steps:

  1. Split the OCR text. Divide the input into manageable chunks.
  2. Request corrections. Send each chunk as text to the model and receive proposed repairs.
  3. Validate the output. Run deterministic checks before accepting the proposed changes.

The validation layer checks three things:

  • Digits: If the model changes any digits, the proposed correction is rejected—even if the replacement seems plausible.
  • Capitalized words: A correction is rejected if it introduces a new capitalized word.
  • Text similarity: A correction is rejected if its similarity to the original falls below a threshold of 0.80.

These rules are intentionally cautious. A model might produce a fluent sentence while quietly changing a name, number, or other important detail. Fluency alone isn't enough to make a correction trustworthy.

There are limitations, though. The model only receives OCR text; it never sees the original page image to verify a suspected error. Inference also relies on a hosted API, so this isn't an offline or private-inference solution.

My latest test run reported 32 passing tests and 6 failures. The remaining failures involve plausible-repair behavior, retry-cap fallback, and repeated-chunk caching. The validation thresholds have also only been tested on a small sample, so they need broader evaluation.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation makes it easier for developers to experiment with models, inspect their behavior, and build tools around them instead of treating AI as a black box.

For this project, working with Gemma gave me a way to explore model-assisted OCR correction while keeping the surrounding validation logic under my control.

The distinction matters: the model proposes a correction, but the application decides whether to accept it.

This project still uses a hosted API, so it isn't fully independent of a closed service. But using an open model gives the project a path toward further experimentation, including evaluating different models and exploring alternative inference setups.

For me, open innovation isn't just about making a model available. It's also about giving developers room to question its output, test its limitations, and build safeguards around it.

The Spirit of It

There's something interesting about working with text from an old newspaper.

A single character can change a name. A digit can change a date. A small correction can quietly become a new error if nobody checks it.

Late Edition doesn't solve historical OCR correction, and it can't verify a transcription against the original scan. But building it made me think more carefully about the difference between text that looks right and text that has actually been checked.

Sometimes, the most important part of an AI-assisted system Is knowing when not to make one.

Thanks to the organizers and everyone building and sharing projects through the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge. 🚀

These rules are intentionally cautious. A model might produce a fluent sentence while quietly changing a name, number, or other important detail. Fluency alone isn't enough to make a correction trustworthy.

There are limitations, though. The model only receives OCR text; it never sees the original page image to verify a suspected error. Inference also relies on a hosted API, so this isn't an offline or private-inference solution.

My latest test run reported 32 passing tests and 6 failures. The remaining failures involve plausible-repair behavior, retry-cap fallback, and repeated-chunk caching. The validation thresholds have also only been tested on a small sample, so they need broader evaluation.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation makes it easier for developers to experiment with models, inspect their behavior, and build tools around them instead of treating AI as a black box.

For this project, working with Gemma gave me a way to explore model-assisted OCR correction while keeping the surrounding validation logic under my control.

The distinction matters: the model proposes a correction, but the application decides whether to accept it.

This project still uses a hosted API, so it isn't fully independent of a closed service. But using an open model gives the project a path toward further experimentation, including evaluating different models and exploring alternative inference setups.

For me, open innovation isn't just about making a model available. It's also about giving developers room to question its output, test its limitations, and build safeguards around it.

The Spirit of It

There's something interesting about working with text from an old newspaper.

A single character can change a name. A digit can change a date. A small correction can quietly become a new error if nobody checks it.

Late Edition doesn't solve historical OCR correction, and it can't verify a transcription against the original scan. But building it made me think more carefully about the difference between text that looks right and text that has actually been checked.

Sometimes, the most important part of an AI-assisted system Is knowing when not to make one.

title: Three documents that keep my AI coding agent honest (free templates + Claude Code skill)
summary:
I run a one-person R&D operation that ships industrial sensing products — analogue boards, microcontroller firmware, PC tools. Most of the typing is done by AI coding agents (mainly Claude Code). They are fast, and for a year they failed in the same four ways:

  • They extended the scope without asking.
  • They reported "done" without running the test.
  • They stated facts they had not checked ("the sibling project uses the same part").
  • They repeated the same mistake in the next session.

None of this was fixed by a better model. It was fixed by a process the agent cannot skip. I've generalized it into a small kit and put it on GitHub under MIT: ai-rd-process-kit.

The idea

Before any implementation, the agent writes three documents, and I accept them:

  1. Plan — scope decided in seven lines (constraints, vision, first release, one-sentence core concept, out of scope, MVP, deferred), completion criteria before the task list, and a progress scale where 100% means reviewed and tested, nothing else.
  2. Design document — every chapter created on day one. A chapter that doesn't apply says "N/A (reason)". Rejected options are kept with the reason. Design order is data → functions → UI, because starting from the screen is how you find the missing data at the end.
  3. Requirements ↔ test matrix — every requirement has at least one test, every pass criterion is a number, and "not run" is a status that is never reported as "pass".

Then the agent works in small checked pieces, updates the documents in the same change that alters the design, and when it fails, it writes the lesson itself: situation, cause, prevention. It reads that file at the start of every session.

The progress scale (the part people copy first)

% Means
0 Not started
25 Started
50 Draft complete, not self-checked
75 Waiting for review, or under test
100 Accepted in review and tests passed

Unverified work stays at 75. Where things can be counted, they are counted: tests passed 38/52 → 73%.

Two real lessons from the file

"Not found" is not "does not exist." The agent searched a rulebook for two keywords, found nothing, and reported that no rule applied. The rule existed under different wording. Prevention: questions of the form "is there a rule about X" are answered by reading the relevant chapters, and the report says what was searched and what was not read.

ERC passed, the netlist had three shorts. An auto-generated schematic passed the electrical rules check. The netlist showed a rotated protection diode shorting two supply rails, a pull-up routed onto a data line, and a duplicated reference designator. Prevention: after generating a schematic, export the netlist and script-check supply/ground separation, polarity of oriented parts and duplicate designators before layout.

What's in the kit

  • templates/ — plan, design doc, requirements↔test matrix, lessons-learned (with four real, anonymized examples)
  • rules/CLAUDE.md.example — 13 promises for the root of your project
  • skills/rd-process/SKILL.md — a Claude Code skill: session start, create the docs, work, test, log, session end

Five-minute setup: copy the templates into docs/, put the rules in CLAUDE.md, install the skill, and say "plan this". If the agent starts coding before showing you the scope table, the rules aren't loaded.

What it is not

Not a methodology, not a tool, not a prompt pack. Four Markdown files and a habit. It works with any agent that reads an instruction file; the skill is for Claude Code.

If you try it, I'd like to know which rule your agent broke first. Mine was #4.

Disclosure: this post and the templates were drafted with an AI assistant and rewritten by me from first-hand use.

title: Ghost in the Code: Offline Séance with Programming Language Spirits
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4 — Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Ghost in the Code — Every language leaves a ghost behind.

It is a local-first educational game that feels like an abandoned computer coming back to life. You summon fictional spirits inspired by historical programming languages — COBOL, BASIC, and Assembly — inside a phosphor-green haunted terminal. They teach, tease, and help you Exorcise the Bug: curated debugging mysteries with deterministic scoring.

The defining constraint: after you install Ollama and pull the model, core play works without the internet. There is no cloud AI fallback. Prompts stay on your machine. Progress, XP, quests, relics, and chat history live in localStorage.

This is the challenge’s own idea made literal — “an offline séance chatbot that channels the spirit of a long-dead programming language” — turned into a playable RPG rather than a themed chatbot skin.

What you can do

  • Boot the CRT terminal, summon a ghost, and talk about programming / computing history
  • Solve six local debugging cases (loops, conditionals, state, recursion) with hint penalties
  • Earn XP, levels, titles, combos, daily streaks, ghost affinity, quests, and unlockable relic themes
  • Hear procedural Web Audio (no sound files, no CDN media)
  • Fail safely: model output is plain text; answers are never eval’d or shelled out

Default model: qwen2.5:1.5b (~986 MB, Apache-2.0) — chosen for a GTX 1050 Ti / 16 GB RAM class machine. Swap via .env.

Demo

This is intentionally not a hosted SaaS demo. Judges (and you) run it locally:

Repo: https://github.com/arjankc/ghost-in-the-code

git clone https://github.com/arjankc/ghost-in-the-code.git
cd ghost-in-the-code
copy .env.example .env
npm install
ollama pull qwen2.5:1.5b
npm run dev

Open http://127.0.0.1:5173

Three-minute path:

  1. Finish the boot sequence (click / Enter) — audio unlocks on first gesture
  2. Confirm LOCAL AI READY, summon COBOL, ask why teams rewrite working systems
  3. Open Exorcise the Bug → The Off-By-One Lanterns → hint optional → submit day <= 10
  4. Watch score burst, XP pop, quest/achievement chatter in the Chronicle
  5. (Optional offline proof) disconnect Wi‑Fi and send another prompt — Ollama on 127.0.0.1:11434 still answers

No login. No API keys. If Ollama is missing, the setup screen explains the gap instead of silently calling a cloud model.

How I Built It

Week 4’s theme is thin places between past and present. Programming languages are that: COBOL still runs ledgers; BASIC taught a generation; Assembly still lurks under everything polite. I wanted players to feel that history without pretending the model has real memories — every generated reply is labeled as fiction.

Local AI as the product, not a badge

Hardware was the design brief: NVIDIA GTX 1050 Ti (4 GB) and 16 GB RAM. That ruled out “just pull a 7B and hope.” Defaulting to qwen2.5:1.5b kept CPU/partial-GPU inference realistic. The app never auto-downloads multi‑GB weights; the README and setup screen ask the human to run ollama pull.

Architecture stays boring on purpose:

  • Vite + React UI on localhost
  • Tiny Express API bound to 127.0.0.1
  • Ollama only at a configured local URL — clients cannot inject a remote endpoint

That pattern matches what local-AI builders keep rediscovering: a thin Node bridge to Ollama is enough for private, offline chat without renting a cloud brain (privacy-first local assistant writeups on DEV; offline AI stacks that actually run today).

Game first, model second for fairness

Small models are wonderful séance partners and terrible judges. So Exorcise the Bug uses version-controlled puzzles and string-normalized validators. Hints can be narrated by the ghost; score is always deterministic (100 / 75 / 50 / 25). That keeps the educational loop honest when the spirit rambles.

Then I leaned into gamification — still 100% local:

  • XP, levels, titles, combos, daily streaks
  • Ghost affinity meters
  • Quest board + achievements
  • Unlockable relic themes (cosmetic CRT palettes)
  • Chronicle / stats HUD
  • Boot sequence, typewriter replies, procedural audio (no asset licensing rabbit hole — same idea as Web Audio–only game SFX)

Safety rails

  • No eval, no shelling model output, no arbitrary code execution
  • Plain-text rendering of AI replies
  • Clear distinction between curated history-inspired fiction and verified facts in character prompts
  • App code MIT; model weights documented separately (1.5B Apache-2.0; optional qwen2.5:3b is a different research license)

Why Open Innovation Matters

It works when the network doesn’t. Classrooms, travel, flaky ISP nights — once Ollama and the weights are on disk, the séance continues. A closed chat API simply goes dark.

Prompts stay on the laptop. Students asking “dumb” debugging questions shouldn’t have to ship that insecurity to a vendor. Local inference keeps the conversation co-located with the shame and the learning.

No per-token bill for the core loop. Electricity and disk still cost something — local is not free — but there is no surprise invoice for every COBOL monologue.

The brain is swappable. Change OLLAMA_MODEL and restart. The game, puzzles, and UI do not care which compatible open-weight instruction model you prefer. That is the opposite of rebuilding around one commercial assistant’s deprecation calendar.

Inspectable pedagogy. Characters, prompts, scoring, and quests are ordinary TypeScript/JSON in the repo. Teachers and curious students can fork a ghost or add a case without asking permission from an API product manager.

Closed tools are fine for many jobs. For a haunted classroom terminal that must keep working offline, open weights + open code were not a branding choice — they were the only architecture that matched the fantasy.

Prize Categories

None claimed for partner tracks this week — the project’s open core is local Ollama + Qwen2.5, not a featured partner runtime. Happy to compete on the overall Ghost in the Machine criteria: theme fit, local open-weight inference, and a write-up that shows the work.

If you try it, summon Assembly and ask something vague on purpose. It will make you be precise. The ledger prefers that.

title: Why Static System Design Diagrams Lie (And How I Built a 60 FPS Distributed Systems Simulator in the Browser)
summary:
Every architecture review I've ever sat in goes roughly the same way. Someone opens Excalidraw or draw.io, draws a rectangle labeled API, draws an arrow to Redis, draws another arrow to Postgres, and everyone nods and says "looks solid, ship it."

Then two weeks later traffic spikes 3x, Redis is chilling at 2ms, Postgres is at 99% CPU dropping connections, and retries from the API gateway turn a minor slowdown into a full outage.

The problem with static diagrams is that a 2,500 RPS cache and a 400 RPS database look like the exact same box on a screen. Boxes don't have queues. Lines don't drop packets.

Over the past few weeks I've been building GraphFlow to fix that. It's an open-source system design canvas where the diagram actually runs in your browser.

If you want to skip the text and just poke at it, here is a live model of a Stripe-style webhook & double-entry ledger setup (no login or signup):

👉 Open the live Stripe Ledger simulation

Once it opens, try two things:

  1. Grab the Load slider in the top bar and drag it from 1x to 3.5x. Watch the utilization bar under the Postgres node turn red while p99 latency shoots up.
  2. Click on any database or worker node and hit Kill (or +100ms) in the little floating bar above it. You'll see red 5xx packets back up until the upstream circuit breaker trips OPEN to stop the bleeding.

There's also a Netflix edge streaming chaos setup and a CQRS + Kafka Outbox template if you want to play with different topologies.

How the queuing math works (without melting the browser)

I didn't want the moving dots to just be eye candy. In GraphFlow, packets only spawn at actual ingress nodes (like a client, mobile app, or webhook source) and travel hop-by-hop. A downstream node doesn't emit a packet until an upstream packet actually reaches it.

Every node has a base latency, a max RPS capacity, and an error rate. When incoming traffic stays below ~70% of a node's capacity, latency stays flat. Once you cross 75% utilization, queuing backpressure kicks in and tail latency (p95 / p99) curves upward fast:

const utilization = Math.min(1.5, arrivalRps / Math.max(1, node.throughputRps));
const queuingMultiplier =
  utilization > 0.75
    ? 1 + Math.pow((utilization - 0.75) / 0.25, 2) * 2.8
    : 1 + utilization * 0.25;

If a node has a circuit breaker enabled and hits 5 consecutive 5xx failures, it trips OPEN for 6 seconds, drops into HALF-OPEN to test the waters with a single request, and closes again if the downstream service recovered. You can also dial up packet loss (0% to 50%) on individual wires to see what happens when the network between two healthy services gets flaky.

Avoiding heavy canvas libraries (and the 2.5-Gigapixel mobile bug)

Initially I considered using PixiJS or Konva for the canvas, but I wanted crisp DOM text, normal CSS styling, and a tiny bundle. So the entire canvas is just standard React DOM nodes + native SVG cubic Bezier paths, evaluated via De Casteljau's formula inside a requestAnimationFrame loop.

To keep React from choking at 60 FPS, the simulation loop reads from mutable refs (nodesRef / edgesRef) and an O(1) lookup map instead of triggering full canvas re-renders on every tick.

That worked great on my desktop, until I opened the site on my phone last week and watched mobile Safari drop to about 4 FPS.

title: A rental yield calculator should show the scenario that loses money
summary:
A positive rental yield is easy to demonstrate with a friendly input. The more useful question for a property-data tool is what happens when occupancy falls while fixed costs and loan payments remain due.

We added a browser-based Rental Cashflow Stress Lab to our existing open-source calculator. It compares explicit scenarios instead of replacing uncertain inputs with country presets.

This is a project from NovAsia Estate, where our property research covers Cambodia, Thailand and Bali. All the figures below are synthetic test inputs, not observations about those markets.

Keep capacity rent separate from collected rent

The input we call full-occupancy rent is a capacity assumption:

scenario capacity = full-occupancy annual rent × rent-level multiplier
collected annual rent = scenario capacity × occupancy

For example, 24,000 at 70% occupancy becomes 16,800 of collected annual rent. A downside scenario uses a lower rent level of 85% and occupancy of 35%, giving 7,140.

This simple annual fraction does not model seasonality, cancellation patterns or the difference between asking and achieved rent. Making that limitation explicit is preferable to presenting the result as a forecast.

Fixed costs should survive zero occupancy

Our example has 1,200 of annual common-area charges, 500 of other fixed costs and 6,000 of annual debt service. Management and maintenance-reserve assumptions are 20% and 5% of collected rent.

The core engine calculates operating income and applies the caller's chosen simplified tax base. The stress extension subtracts debt service afterwards. It does not infer tax deductibility of interest, depreciation, a loan balance or an equity-return denominator.

With an illustrative 10% tax on positive operating profit, the three fixture outcomes are:

Scenario Occupancy Rent level Fixed-cost level Net annual cash flow after debt
Base 70% 100% 100% 3,810
Vacancy shock 35% 85% 125% -3,093
Stronger demand 90% 110% 100% 8,508

At zero occupancy, those original fixed costs and debt still produce a loss of 7,700. The tool retains that number. A missing cost is an input error; zero must be entered deliberately.

Break-even needs the same assumptions as the comparison

Let F be fixed operating costs, D annual debt service, k the fraction of collected rent remaining after management and reserve, and t the supplied tax rate.

For a gross-rent tax assumption, the continuous threshold is (F + D) / (k - t) when the retained margin is positive.

For tax on positive operating profit, with k > 0 and t < 1, it is (F + D / (1 - t)) / k.

The example's base case needs about 11,155.56 of collected annual rent, or about 46.48% of its stated capacity. A requirement above 100% occupancy means the entered rent capacity cannot cover the costs. Impossible margins and zero capacity have explicit states rather than a misleading percentage. The exact edge cases, including 100% tax and zero costs, are covered by tests.

These thresholds are approximate continuous results before cent rounding. Breaking even is not the same as earning a positive return.

Keep the experiment reproducible

The extension uses the same engine as the original calculator:

const Stress = require('./docs/stress.js');
const input = require('./examples/stress.json');
const report = Stress.compare(
  input.base,
  input.annualDebtService,
  input.scenarios
);
console.log(report.rows.map(row => [row.name, row.netAfterDebt]));

The source repository contains the fixture and 36 passing contracts, including zero rent, retained losses, both tax bases, impossible break-even states, CSV formula protection and browser/Node consistency. JSON exports retain the assumptions and itemized core results. Browser inputs are calculated locally without upload requests.

For the earlier acquisition stage, our Payment Milestone Studio allocates dated installments with exact integer arithmetic. That is a separate problem: a purchase payment schedule does not establish rental income.

The Stress Lab is a repository and browser extension. The published novasia-sea-yield npm package remains version 2.0.1; we are not describing unshipped npm exports. Contributions that make assumptions clearer are welcome.

title: 5 Free Insurance Broker Software Tools in 2026 (Honest Review)
summary:
If you run a brokerage or work as a solo producer you already know the software market is heavily stacked against small firms.

Standard Agency Management Systems like Applied Epic, EZLynx or AMS360 generally charge between $150 and $500 per month per user. On top of subscription fees many vendors lock your data into their proprietary cloud systems charge onboarding fees and require multi-year contracts. For an agency writing commercial and personal lines sinking $3,000 to $6,000 annually into software licenses before turning a profit is a serious burden.

Fortunately several free and open-source alternatives exist for agencies looking to keep costs low. Below is an honest breakdown of the five free tools available in 2026 their strengths and their real-world limitations.

Comparison Overview

| Tool License / Cost | Data Storage | Insurance Focus | Primary Use Case |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| PelSure Free lifetime | Local SQLite (Offline) | Purpose-built for brokers Solo brokers & small independent agencies

| Odoo Community | Open-source (Free) | Self-hosted database | Generic ERP | Agencies with in-house technical resources |

| JenesisClassic | Free basic tier | On-premise server | Purpose-built for P&C | Small agencies needing basic policy tracking |

| SuiteCRM. Open-source (Free) | Self-hosted database | Generic sales CRM | Brokers focused strictly on pipelines |

| InsuredMine Free trial | Cloud SaaS | Purpose-built CRM | Agencies testing marketing automation workflows |

1. PelSure

PelSure is a Windows desktop suite designed specifically for independent brokers who want to operate without recurring software fees or cloud data dependencies.

How it works:

Unlike web-based CRMs PelSure operates entirely offline. Client records, policy schedules and quotation files are stored locally on your machine inside an encrypted SQLite database.

Strengths:

  • Complete Data Privacy: Because client records never touch a third-party cloud server the system is inherently compliant with UK GDPR, Singapore MAS guidelines and other regional financial privacy rules.

  • Multi-Carrier Quoting Matrix: Side-by-side premium comparison across Motor, Fire, Marine, Personal Accident and Workmens Compensation.

  • Spreadsheet Migration: A built-in import center allows brokers to transfer existing client books directly from Excel or CSV files with deduplication.

  • WhatsApp Integration: Deep-links directly to desktop WhatsApp to dispatch policy schedules quotes and renewal notices to clients with one click.

  • Resource Efficient: Built using Tauri and React the installer is under 10 MB and operates smoothly on standard office hardware.

Limitations:

  • Platform limited: Currently runs on Windows 10 and Windows 11 (no macOS version yet).

  • No multi-branch cloud sync: Designed for single-machine usage or local setups; not suitable for 50-person distributed brokerages.

Website: https://pelsure.peltelldesignco.com

Installer: Available on SourceForge

2. Odoo Community Edition

Odoo Community is an used open-source ERP system that includes a solid customer relationship management module.

How it works:

You. Install Odoo on your local computer or a self-hosted cloud server (like DigitalOcean or AWS).

Strengths:

  • free with zero user caps.

  • Robust pipeline tracking, invoicing, document attachments and customer communication history.

  • Community app marketplace for extending capabilities.

Limitations:

  • Odoo is an enterprise system, not an insurance platform. It has no understanding of insurance policies, policy renewal cycles, carrier commissions or comparative rating.

  • Requires technical setup and regular database maintenance.

3. Jenesis (JenesisClassic / Basic)

Jenesis has provided software to Property and Casualty agents for over twenty years. While their flagship product is now the cloud-based JenesisNow they still offer entry-level desktop configurations.

How it works:

A traditional Windows-based client management utility tailored to personal and commercial line agents.

Strengths:

  • Purpose-built for insurance agents with standard industry workflows.

  • Good handling of ACORD forms and basic policy history.

  • Built-in client accounting and premium receipt tracking.

Limitations:

  • The free offerings are strictly limited in terms of integrations and record volume.

  • Upgrading to full carrier integration requires transitioning into paid tiers.

4. SuiteCRM

SuiteCRM is an enterprise-grade open-source CRM originally forked from SugarCRM. It is widely used across services.

How it works:

Runs on a LAMP stack (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP). You host it yourself giving you control over the underlying database.

Strengths:

  • Mature, reliable contact management with workflow automation.

  • Ability to create custom modules and custom fields for tracking policy numbers and renewal dates.

  • Strong role-based access controls for multi-agent offices.

Limitations:

  • Requires upfront configuration to make it function like an insurance broker system.

  • Does not offer rating, policy schedule generation or carrier dispatch features.

5. InsuredMine (Trial Tier)

InsuredMine is an agency CRM focused on sales pipeline visibility, client engagement and marketing automation.

How it works:

A cloud-native SaaS application that connects into an agencys existing management workflows.

Strengths:

  • clean user interface with visual pipeline boards.

  • Automated email and SMS nurture sequences for policy renewals and cross-selling.

  • Good reporting dashboards tracking rates and lead sources.

Limitations:

  • Not free. After the trial period agencies must subscribe to paid plans starting at roughly $75 to $120 per user per month.

  • Storing all client data on servers may require formal data protection review depending on your jurisdiction.

Summary and Recommendations

Selecting the tool comes down to your operating model:

  1. For brokers and independent agencies wanting a free private desktop workflow: PelSure provides the out-of-the-box insurance capabilities without recurring costs.

  2. For agencies with IT resources wanting a centralized web database: Odoo Community or SuiteCRM can be customized into a solid administrative backbone.

  3. For growing agencies with a marketing budget: Evaluating commercial platforms, like InsuredMine or JenesisNow is worthwhile once transaction volume justifies the monthly subscription.

title: Offline On-Device AI Agents with Gemma & Local Tool Calls (feat. Shivay Lamba)
summary:
In our latest CodingCat.dev podcast recording, Shivay Lamba (@howdevelop) walked through a practical real-world use case for 100% offline, on-device AI agents in healthcare.

The Problem: Privacy and Latency in Healthcare Prescriptions

When a doctor consults with a patient and writes a prescription, traditional cloud LLM pipelines require sending sensitive patient audio and medical records over the network, or handing the patient a physical slip to wait in line at a pharmacy.

The On-Device Agentic Architecture

Instead of routing sensitive patient conversations to external cloud APIs, Shivay demonstrates a two-stage local workflow running directly on a doctor's laptop or smartphone:
